articles.title: Super Typhoon Rosal slightly strengthens over Philippine Sea
articles.summary: The trough or extension of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) may cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in Bicol and Eastern Visayas on Tuesday evening, October 20

blocks.text: ROSAL. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 20, 2026, 4 pm.
NOAA
The trough or extension of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) may cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in Bicol and Eastern Visayas on Tuesday evening, October 20

items: Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) intensified on Tuesday afternoon, October 20, with maximum sustained winds increasing to 195 km/h.
The super typhoon is not expected to make landfall but will affect parts of the Philippines.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) slightly intensified over the Philippine Sea on Tuesday afternoon, October 20, with its maximum sustained winds again reaching 195 kilometers per hour from the previous 185 km/h.

The super typhoon’s gustiness also increased from 230 km/h to 240 km/h, said the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) in its 5 pm bulletin on Tuesday.
Rosal was last spotted 1,270 kilometers east of Central Luzon at 4 pm, still moving west northwest at 25 km/h. It had entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 10:40 am.

The super typhoon is not expected to make landfall in the Philippines, but it will still affect parts of the country due to its size and intensity. It will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon from Thursday, October 22, to Friday, October 23.
On Tuesday evening, Rosal’s trough or extension may cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in more areas, with the latest forecast now covering the entire regions of Bicol and Eastern Visayas.
From Thursday afternoon to Friday afternoon, or a 24-hour period, these two provinces in Northern Luzon are seen to have significant rain due to Rosal:

items: Heavy to intense rain (100-200 millimeters): Batanes
Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Cagayan

blocks.text: For now, Batanes, along with Ilocos Norte and Babuyan Islands, will just have isolated light rain due to the northeasterly windflow.
Meanwhile, more areas were placed under Signal No. 1 as of 5 pm on Tuesday, which means they should prepare for strong winds from the super typhoon:

items: Batanes
Babuyan Islands
northern part of Ilocos Norte (Pagudpud)

northern and eastern parts of mainland Cagayan (Santa Ana, Gonzaga, Lal-lo, Santa Teresita, Camalaniugan, Aparri, Buguey, Gattaran, Baggao, Peñablanca, Santa Praxedes, Claveria, Sanchez-Mira, Pamplona, Ballesteros, Abulug, Allacapan)
northeastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan)
northeastern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

blocks.text: The highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal due to Rosal is Signal No. 2 or 3.
The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:
Tuesday, October 20

items: Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Cagayan, Isabela, Polillo Islands, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes, Northern Samar, Eastern Samar, most of Caraga, Camiguin, Misamis Oriental, Sarangani, Davao del Sur, Davao Occidental

blocks.text: Wednesday, October 21

items: Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Polillo Islands, Bicol, Romblon, Eastern Visayas, Iloilo, Guimaras, Negros Occidental, Siquijor, Bohol, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Region, Sarangani, Zamboanga del Norte

blocks.text: Thursday, October 22

items: most of the country

blocks.text: Seaboards affected by Rosal will gradually see worsening conditions. Here is PAGASA’s updated forecast for the next 24 hours:
Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

items: Northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes; seaboard of Isabela; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan; southeastern seaboard of Batanes; northeastern seaboard of Babuyan Islands – waves up to 4.5 meters high

blocks.text: Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

items: Northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes; remaining eastern seaboards of Babuyan Islands and mainland Cagayan; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte and Camarines Sur; northern and eastern seaboards of Northern Samar and Eastern Samar; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon – waves up to 4 meters high

Seaboards of Ilocos Norte and Ilocos Sur; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining northern and eastern seaboards of Camarines Sur; remaining seaboards of Polillo Islands, Dinagat Islands, and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group – waves up to 2 meters high

blocks.text: PAGASA said Rosal will move generally west northwest until Wednesday, October 21, before heading generally northwest until Friday morning. Afterwards, it may turn north northwest to north starting Friday afternoon, until it leaves PAR by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24.
The weather bureau also sees possible intensification in the coming hours as Rosal moves over the Philippine Sea, but it could weaken into a typhoon on Thursday evening or early Friday morning.
Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Landmark Cowichan Nation appeal sparks warnings of 'chaotic situation'
articles.summary: The province, the City of Richmond, the Port of Vancouver and a pair of First Nations are all warning that dire consequences could flow from a controversial land title decision granting the Cowichan…

image.caption: A controversial B.C. Supreme Court decision involving Aboriginal title and private property in the Richmond area is headed to B.C.'s highest court. In submissions obtained by CBC News, the province and other parties are warning of dire consequences. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: The province of B.C. claims public confidence in the land registration system and the "essential work of reconciliation" is in peril.
Meanwhile, the City of Richmond says the "property of thousands of Richmond's citizens" could be at risk in the event of catastrophic flooding.
The Port of Vancouver claims port operations, leaseholders and businesses employing hundreds of people could face a "chaotic situation."
And both the Musqueam Indian Band and Tsawwassen First Nation say they're being squeezed out of their traditional fishing grounds.

items: 'It would be wrong': Why Richmond, B.C., residents weren't told about First Nation's claim to title

blocks.text: CBC News has obtained copies of lengthy submissions filed in B.C.'s Court of Appeal earlier this month, in multiple bids to stay parts of the landmark B.C. Supreme Court Quw'utsun (Cowichan) Nation Aboriginal title decision before it comes into full effect in February 2027.

Six of the parties appealing the ruling claim dire consequences could flow from Justice Barbara Young's decision — which they claim impacts dikes, private property, a port transporation hub and the right to fish in waters claimed by other First Nations.

To that end, the province, Canada's attorney general, the port, the City of Richmond and the Musqueam and Tsawwassen Nations will be in court in January asking for a freeze on certain parts of the ruling while the full appeal process plays out.
The Quw'utsun Nation have yet to file their response to the claims, but their lawyer told CBC News "they have solutions to each and every one" of the alleged harms.
Fallout from a landmark ruling

The documents include affidavits from executives about the uncertainty hanging over the Port of Vancouver, as well as a First Nations fisheries co-ordinator who claims "Cowichan fishing vessels were in the south arm [of the Fraser River] the day after the trial decision was released."

The more than 5,000 pages of filings also contain the back and forth between a lawyer for the province and a lawyer for the Quw'utsun over the definition of the term "private landowners" — and the question of legal action against future purchasers of the affected land.

The Cowichan decision is heading to the province's highest court as an election plays out. From left: B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby and B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

"Justice Young was speaking of 'the private fee simple title holders' as of the date of judgment. Your definition purports to define private landowners to include those who acquire their interest post-judgment," the Quw'utsun lawyer wrote to his counterpart for the Crown.

"You define private landowners in your letter in a way that does not restrict the definition in any temporal sense so that it would include future purchasers from present landowners in the Cowichan Title lands ... The Quw'utsun Nation has not and does not resile from protecting its Aboriginal title in future litigation regarding the Cowichan Title lands."

items: B.C. and Cowichan chiefs start negotiations after court ruling on Aboriginal title

blocks.text: The relationship between Aboriginal title and private property dominated headlines following the initial release of Young's decision in August 2025, but the appeal court documents show just how consequential the rest of the ruling promises to be.

Taken as a whole, the arguments provide a detailed window into one of the most contentious issues facing British Columbia — one playing out in the province's highest court even as the politicians vying to lead B.C. head into an election this weekend.
Ruling steeped in history

Young's decision established Aboriginal title for the Quw'utsun over up to 325 hectares (800 acres) of riverside property and submerged land in Richmond owned by the federal Crown, the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority, the City of Richmond and private landowners.
The 600-page ruling also declared the Quw'utsun's Aboriginal right to fish for food in the south arm of of the Fraser River — traditional territory for both the Musqueam and Tsawwassen.
In 1859, British Columbia's first governor — James Douglas — promised to set aside the land claimed by the Quw'utsun from sale or claims from settlers. (B.C. Archives/Wikipedia)

Young delved into the history of the area to conclude the Crown lacked authority to sell or distribute the land — set aside long ago by B.C.'s first governor as the site of a traditional Quw'utsun village.

While the Quw'utsun said they weren't asking the judge to invalidate ownership of the dozens of private properties covered by the ruling, Young addressed the issue regardless, responding to arguments raised by Richmond and the province on behalf of private landowners.
The judge said the Quw'utsun's Aboriginal title extends to the privately-owned property — held through what is known in law as "fee simple."

But she suggested the two forms of title can coexist, saying “the property rights of the private landowners are not undermined.” The judge said it would be up to the Crown and the Quw'utsun to "negotiate and reconcile" Aboriginal title and private interests.

items: 'Cloud' of tension between Aboriginal title and private property ownership lands in B.C.

blocks.text: The province, Canada's attorney general, the Port of Vancouver, the City of Richmond, the Musqueam Indian Band and the Tsawwassen First Nation all appealed — as did the Quw'utsun, who had originally sought Aboriginal title to a much larger area.

The portion of the decision implicating private property and fishing rights went into immediate effect, but Young suspended the parts affecting the port and the City of Richmond for 18 months to give the parties time to deal with the fallout from her decision.
But with that Feb. 7 deadline fast approaching, it's clear from the Appeal Court proceedings the matter is far from settled.
A heyday for lawyers
Arguments on the appeals themselves are set to begin in November 2027.

But first, the court will meet in January to decide on six stay applications — which argue that allowing Young's ruling to come into full effect before the appeal court has reached a final decision would cause "irreparable harm."

Lawyers for all parties gathered in a sixth-floor courtroom in downtown Vancouver last Thursday for a case management conference, with the Appeal Court registrar tasked with wrangling dates, schedules and material for the judges who will ultimately decide the case.
The interior of a courtroom is shown at the B.C. Supreme Court building where lawyers have been meeting in the lead-up to appeal court proceedings related to the Quw'utsun decision. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
More than a dozen lawyers — most in person, some appearing virtually — easily outnumbered the handful of people in the public gallery.
The registrar told the lawyers they could dispense with some formalities: "We'll be here all afternoon if we introduce ourselves."
A intense phalanx of suited lawyers shuffled in and out of the courtroom as they huddled to come up with a proposed schedule for filings.
In total, eight separate but related appeal cases have been filed — seven from the original parties, and another from a landowner who lost a bid to reopen the Supreme Court proceedings this summer.

items: Lawsuit attempting to reopen Cowichan Aboriginal title case dismissed

blocks.text: Further complicating the proceedings: an as-yet-unknown number of intervenors.

The court file includes a letter from a lawyer for the Independent Contractors and Business Association (ICBA), asking to intervene on behalf of 5,000 members in the construction and development industry — a number of whom have interests in the claim area.

"Should leave be granted, ICBA expects to address the implications of the trial decision from the perspective of the construction and development industry, which relies on aspects of the land title system," the letter says.
In addition, a lawyer for the province told the registrar he has been contacted by "what I would call 10 serious potential intervenors."
New Cowichan documents warn of far-reaching impacts of landmark court case
Irreparable harms?
Because of the unprecedented nature of the issues at play, the Crown is seeking a hearing by a special panel of five Appeal Court justices instead of the normal three-judge panel.

Each of the stay applications seeks a halt to different parts of Young's rulings: the declaration of fishing rights, Aboriginal title over certain fee-simple lands owned by Richmond and Aboriginal title over the Port of Vancouver lands.
The province also wants an order stopping the Cowichan from taking steps to enforce their title against the private property owners.
In each case, the judges have to decide if a serious legal issue exists, whether real, "irreparable" harm is threatened and — crucially — how the risks to each side balance out.

The ruling established Aboriginal title for the Quw'utsun over up to 325 hectares of riverside property and submerged land in Richmond owned by the federal Crown, the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority, the City of Richmond and private landowners. (CBC News)
The Quw'utsun have yet to file their responses to the stay applications. The registrar gave them a mid-December deadline.
At the case management conference, Quw'utsun lawyer David Rosenberg noted the "avalanche" of material facing his clients.

items: B.C. and Cowichan chiefs start negotiations after court ruling on Aboriginal title

blocks.text: In an email to CBC News, the veteran lawyer provided a broad outline of his client's position.
"There have been many inaccurate statements made by politicians about this case, and those statements have caused unnecessary fear and anxiety," Rosenberg wrote.

"The truth is that anyone who is familiar with the history in this case knows that it is exceptional in many ways and does not have general application to either all claimed [Aboriginal] title lands or all private property," he added.
Each submission makes a distinct set of arguments.
The province and public angst

The province's filings speak directly to public debate surrounding Young's decision, including a list of newspaper articles with headlines like, "It's Scary;" "This Land is Not Your Land" and "Canada's $1 Billion Question: Do Property Rights Still Exist in British Columbia?"
The court documents say the decision has "cast serious doubt" on the rights of private landowners.

Richmond resident Kal Matt is seen raising frustrations over the notification process about the Cowichan Tribes Aboriginal title case, during a town hall meeting on Oct. 28, 2025. (Glen Kugelstadt/CBC)

"The province has requested clarity and assurance from the Cowichan that no steps will be taken to enforce or exercise Aboriginal title against private landowners pending a determination of the appeal," the province says in its arguments.

"However to date, the Cowichan have declined this request. This refusal has left private landowners — and the public generally — facing a present spectre of direct action, including litigation, by the Cowichan."

items: B.C. attorney general, Cowichan Nation lawyers welcome Supreme Court decision on N.B. case

blocks.text: The province says it's charged "with promoting and protecting the public interest in myriad ways, including through maintenance of a reliable provincial system of land registration and through undertaking the challenging but essential work of reconciliation."

"The threat of litigation over the non-party private lands, the significant uncertainty resulting from the trial court's findings ... and the imminent invalidation of some registered interests ... are not conducive to negotiation or reconciliation," claims the province.
Uncertainty at the port

The Attorney General of Canada and the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority (VFPA) both filed sets of submissions warning of the potential impact of Young's decisions on large sections of the claim area operated and managed by the port authority.
The VFPA says the area the port manages contains "strategically-located industrial lands, uniquely placed to support integrated port operations and facilitate international trade."
"The lands include rail infrastructure, regional roads, office buildings, warehousing and transloading facilities and container storage areas," the court documents read.
The Port of Vancouver claims the land it manages in Richmond is part of infrastructure 'uniquely placed to support integrated port operations and facilitate international trade.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)
The submissions include an affidavit from Tanjit Kalhar, chief executive officer of Euro Asia Transload Inc., a company that leases 21.4 hectares (53 acres) at the Richmond terminal.
"It handles cargo such as liquor, tires, electronics, pulp, paper, steel coils, lumber and Amazon products," the affidavit reads.
"Operations at the terminal play a vital role in the British Columbian and Canadian supply chain an economy."
The court filings include letters the Quw'utsun sent to Kalhar and other business owners inviting them to submit "a detailed proposal to replace" the current leases they have with the port.
But Kalhar claims the uncertainty threatens the long-term stability of the business, which employs hundreds of people.
An affidavit included in the Port of Vancouver's submissions from a leaseholder claims the uncertainty over the Cowichan Tribes case is affecting operations. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
The attorney general's submissions echo that point.

"The uncertainty will have further knock-on effects on associated customers and suppliers, transportation providers, and other port users whose operations are connected to business that operate on these lands within the Port of Vancouver," the arguments read.

"The ability of all these businesses to continue operating on the Canada lands would be at risk. There is currently no suitable alternative location for these port operations and, even if there were, relocation would be a major undertaking that would cause significant disruption and come with a direct financial cost."
Beyond those points, the port authority also raises questions about the aspects of Young's decision finding Aboriginal title on fee simple land — including federal property.
"The trial order undermines public confidence in the ability of Parliament to invest in Canada's ports in the public interest," the court documents say.
Richmond's flood fears

While Richmond's broader appeal concerns multiple aspects of Young's decision, the city's stay application centres on pair of shoreline lots on the south arm of the Fraser River that Richmond acquired in the 1930s when the previous owners failed to pay municipal taxes.
According to the city's submissions, the lots in question contain parts of a perimeter dike that protects the "flat-and low-lying" region from "sea level rise, storm surge, freshet and rainfall."
The City of Richmond says it needs access a perimeter dike and pump station through land located on the Quw'utsun claim area in order to protect residents from floods. (Maryse Zeidler/CBC)
The lots also allegedly provide access to a pump station which moves floodwater out of the city and into the Fraser River or the sea.
The court documents claim the pump station requires weekly — and sometimes daily — inspections to "ensure that it does not present any flooding risk or other safety hazard to the public."
Richmond says it does not have authority to unilaterally enter private land to maintain or inspect dikes.
City of Richmond lawyers argue the B.C. Supreme Court ruling could jeopardize dikes and flood safety. (Steven Chua/CBC)
The city says it has reached agreements with other landowners resulting in legally guaranteed access to the property, but claims that kind of deal is "facially incompatible" with Young's ruling.
The city says it's looking for a "tailored stay" to "ensure that Richmond is in a position to adequately maintain critical flood-protection" pending a final decision on the appeal.
"The safety and property of thousands of Richmond's citizens who are not parties to this litigation ... would be at risk if the city cannot mobilize immediately," the city argues.
First Nations' fish stocks under threat

The Musqueam Indian Band and the Tsawwassen First Nation make similar arguments in their stay applications, which seek to stay Young's declaration of the Cowichan's right to fish in the south arm of the Fraser.
Both the Musqueam and the Tsawwassen recount their history in the area.

The Musqueam Indian Band and the Tsawwassen First Nation claim the Cowichan are squeezing them out of areas where they traditionally fish for salmon. The First Nations are asking for a stay of a Supreme Court decision pending appeal. (CBC)

The Musqueam claim they have lived along the region's waterways for more than 8,000 years and "have engaged in a fishing practice that has provided sustenance as well as cultural foundations persisting into the present day."
The Tsawwassen say they "are a fishing people and their identity is tied to the Fraser River and the sea."

Both groups claim their ability to fish for food, social and ceremonial purposes "was already severely constrained," pointing to the "sustained decline" of Fraser River fish stocks in the years prior to Young's decision.
Both the Musqueam and the Tsawwassen claim the Quw'utsun ruling has placed an already threatened resource at further risk — singling out an alleged threat to the Chinook salmon population.
"Immediately following the release of the trial decision, members of the Cowichan Nation began fishing in the south arm without consulting Musqueam and without its consent," the Musqueam claim.
"The increased number of boats in the south arm due to the presence of the Cowichan Nation are crowding out Musqueam's ability to fish in the narrow section of the river."
The Musqueam and Tsawwassen First Nations claim the Supreme Court ruling is threatening already depleted stocks of Chinook salmon. (Claudiane Samson/Radio-Canada)
The Tsawwassen Fisrt Nation claim they weren't given "notice by the Cowichan or by Canada, let alone consulted, despite holding consultative rights in the Tsawwassen Territory."
"The added vessels mean it takes [Tsawwassen] fishers more time, and costs more to meet their allocation," the Tsawwassen claim.
"And fishing in a more crowded window makes it harder to do so safely."
The Quw'utsun response
The Quw'utsun are expected to file a single response to all six applications by Dec. 18.
Rosenberg gave CBC News a broad outline of the arguments he expects to make.

"For some of them it's simply reaching out to the Cowichan Nation and reaching an agreement so they can — for example — maintain the dikes and the pumping station with our consent and permission," he said.

"Fishing is really a management issue that they should be dealing with Canada and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, but it's not a zero sum game, and Aboriginal rights are not exclusive so it's a shared right and that's the law."

items: Cowichan title lands encompass multimillion-dollar mansions in Richmond, B.C.

blocks.text: Rosenberg said the Port of Vancouver and Canada were given 18 months to arrange a transition "and that's what they should be [focused] on."

The lawyer said he can't discuss ongoing negotiations with the Crown, but he said part of Young's ruling was a declaration that British Columbia has a duty to negotiate in good faith to reconcile the private property interests with Cowichan Aboriginal title.
"The Cowichan will put forward a way in which the Crown acting honourably could protect the Cowichan Title lands and the private property interests," Rosenberg said.

He said it's also important to bear in mind the unique nature of the land in question, which was like "a special reserve that was supposed to be created and was never created and it would not apply to all Aboriginal title land and it wouldn't apply to all fee simple or all private property."

items: Why uncertainty over end result of Cowichan Tribes case invites plenty of speculation

blocks.text: Rosenberg told CBC News he couldn't help but make a final point about the province's application.

"When British Columbia asks to enjoin or prevent the Cowichan Nation from protecting their Aboriginal title lands in future litigation, it harkens back to a dark period in British Columbia history when Indigenous people were not allowed to go to court to protect their rights," he said.
"And that is something that is dishonourable and should be avoided at all costs."

articles.title: Big IPO, big bonus: GCash employees get their own payday
articles.summary: From first-time investors to the country's business elite and the President himself, everyone turned out for GCash. Now, can its record-breaking IPO wake up the sleepy PSE?

blocks.text: From first-time investors to the country's business elite and the President himself, everyone turned out for GCash. Now, can its record-breaking IPO wake up the sleepy PSE?

When no less than the President shows up to ring the bell at your stock market debut, you know it’s a big deal. For GCash employees who have been through the wringer to get the IPO done, there was an even sweeter reason to celebrate.

Sources told Rappler that employees of GCash parent Mynt are getting a prorated P100,000 bonus delivered straight to, you guessed it, their GCash wallets. And it wasn’t just the top brass getting a little something extra, with sources confirming that the payout reached employees across ranks.

Not everyone in Mynt’s nearly 2,600-strong workforce – which helped turn a once-obscure SMS payment service into the homegrown giant it is today – could cram onto the trading floor of the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) Tower. But word has it they held a watch party at their office a few blocks away in BGC, with plenty to cheer about.
Talk about an IPO payday!
On Tuesday, October 20, Mynt pulled off the biggest IPO in Philippine history, raising P60.9 billion and knocking Lucky Me! maker Monde Nissin’s offering in 2021 off the top spot.
And what a crowd it drew.

Among the familiar faces were the Zobel brothers Jaime Augusto and Fernando, Monetary Board member Romeo Bernardo, BPI chief TG Limcaoco, and former transportation secretary turned San Miguel director Jaime Bautista.

The stock market elite was there, too, including PSE chairman Jose Pardo, president Ramon Monzon, and the “dragon lady” Vivian Yuchengco, alongside government bigwigs Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Francis Lim and Finance Secretary Frederick Go.

blocks.caption: LISTED. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (center) leads the bell-ringing for GCash parent Mynt’s IPO. (Left to right) Ayala director Fernando Zobel de Ayala, Mynt CFO Evelyn Ng, Ayala CEO Bong Consing, Ayala chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala, Mynt chairman Ernest Cu, Mynt CEO Martha Sazon, Marc…

blocks.text: And, of course, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself, who hoped the record IPO might finally stir the sleepy beast that is the Philippine stock market.

“We recognize that investors have become more cautious and that attracting fresh capital remains a challenge,” he said. “But Mynt’s initial public offering gives us reason for optimism. The strong interest it has attracted from local and international investors is proof of the continued confidence in Filipino enterprise.”

blocks.caption: Big IPO, big bonus: GCash employees get their own payday

blocks.text: Even on the day of its biggest IPO, the benchmark PSE index ended at around the 5,800 level, practically where it stood at the end of 2012. (READ: PSE enters new territory with GCash’s IPO. But to thrive, it must go further.)

It’s been a rough stretch for the local bourse. Had you put P100 into a fund tracking the Philippine index back then, you’d still have roughly P100 nearly 14 years later, excluding dividends and fees. The same P100 invested in a fund tracking Wall Street’s S&P 500 would now be worth around P830, thanks to US market gains and the weakening peso.
An eightfold gap. That’s how far Philippine stocks have fallen behind.

No wonder GCash’s dealmakers had to work hard to drum up interest. At a post-listing briefing, Mynt investor relations head Jep Tang said the company spent three months courting investors, meeting 137 after filing its registration statement, followed by 213 investor follow-ups and another 110 in the final round.

blocks.caption: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday

blocks.text: On its first day, GCASH climbed as high as P6.76 in the early trading hours before ending its first trading day at P6.60, back where it started. Not the spectacular first-day rally some might have hoped for, but it avoided the dreaded listing day slump, never falling below its offer price.
For now, anyone hoping to collect dividends might have to wait.

“We don’t have instituted a dividend policy yet,” Tang said, pointing instead to the many opportunities where the company intends to put its money to work. (READ: After the IPO party, GCash comes for 5-6 lending next)
Speaking of waiting, what about GCash’s rival Maya?

Maya chairman Manny Pangilinan had earlier floated a 2026 IPO, but the timetable has since slipped to 2027. When Maya cheekily congratulated GCash with a “Congrats, GCash. Welcome to Maya” post featuring the newly listed stock, even the PSE couldn’t resist joining in.
“So, Maya IPO when?”– Rappler.com

articles.title: SC strikes down 2024, 2025 budgets, sets limits for unprogrammed appropriations
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has declared as unconstitutional the General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) for 2024 and 2025 due to budget increases made by Congress, as well as provisions allowing unprogrammed…

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published October 20, 2026 6:56pm

The Supreme Court (SC) has declared as unconstitutional the General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) for 2024 and 2025 due to budget increases made by Congress, as well as provisions allowing unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 budget, the high tribunal said Tuesday.
In a statement, the SC said the ruling found that the 2024 budget was voided due to the P449.5 billion additional unprogrammed appropriations.
The 2025 GAA was likewise struck down because of the additional P17.99 billion for the Special Road Fund.

As for the 2026 GAA, the high court deemed as unconstitutional Special Provisions 1(a) and (b), Chapter XLIII of the 2026 GAA authorizing unprogrammed appropriations. It then set conditions that would allow the such appropriations to be constitutional. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: House bill proposes rice, cash incentives for recyclable waste
articles.summary: A bill filed in the House of Representatives seeks to reward households and organizations with food or cash incentives for turning over recyclable waste.

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026 6:13pm
A bill filed in the House of Representatives seeks to reward households and organizations with food or cash incentives for turning over recyclable waste.

House Bill No. 11146, filed by Rep. Patrick Michael Vargas of Quezon City's 5th District, proposes the "Basura to Ayuda Act," an incentivized solid waste redemption and recovery system that would allow households, homeowners' associations, civic organizations and individuals to exchange non-hazardous recyclable materials for food, groceries or cash.

Under the proposed measure, one kilogram of recyclable plastic could be exchanged for one kilogram of commercial-quality rice or its cash equivalent. One kilogram of metal waste, meanwhile, could be exchanged for two kilograms of rice or its cash equivalent.
“Through this bill, we hit two birds with one stone. We take care of our environment while giving aid to our people,” Vargas said in a statement.
Vargas said the proposal was modeled after the Quezon City government's Trash to Cashback program, which rewards residents for participating in waste management initiatives.

The Philippines generates an estimated 61,000 metric tons of solid waste daily, according to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources. Plastics account for an estimated 12% to 24% of the country's solid waste, based on DENR data.

Under the bill, the DENR, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Industry would be tasked with establishing standardized trade-in centers and ensuring consistent exchange rates across communities.
“Turning waste management into a national habit is essential to safeguarding the environment and securing a healthier future for the country,” Vargas said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Luistro: VP Sara contradicts herself in denying GenCorp. ownership amid SALN declaration
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte is contradicting herself by denying that she owns a Jollibee franchise through GenCorp., House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro said.

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026 6:12pm

Vice President Sara Duterte is contradicting herself by denying that she owns a Jollibee franchise through GenCorp. Industries, Inc., a firm that she declared as one of her business interests in her 2022 and 2023 Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro said.

“We should remember that it was the respondent herself who made her own admission that she is a shareholder of GenCorp. Industries Incorporated. Kita-kita natin lahat. [We all saw her SALN declarations.] I wish to reiterate the jurisprudence which I shared already before the honorable impeachment court, that the court gives more weight to admissions made by public officials,” Luistro said in a press conference.

“It throws [the burden] to the public official to show that that admission is a mistake. [And] as far as we can remember, never pa niya dinispute ‘yung SALN na iyon. Never pa niya dinispute na shareholder talaga siya ng GenCorp Industries Incorporated. If at all, she is saying that ownership of shares does not mean ownership of franchise, that will be for me completely contradictory. You cannot operate Jollibee, unless you are a franchise holder,” Luistro said.
(She never disputed her SALN entries and she never disputed that she is a shareholder of GenCorp.)

Duterte’s shares in GenCorp. is one of the subjects in the unexplained wealth impeachment case against her before the Senate impeachment court, with prosecution witness, lawyer and forensic financial analyst Alex Cabrera testifying that part of the Vice President’s unexplained wealth ranging from P817 million to P1.5 billion is her non-declaration of assets from her shareholding in GenCorp.

Cabrera made the conclusion after a forensic investigation into her joint SALN with her husband, Manases Carpio, as well as the spouses tax, bank deposit, bank transaction and business interests records.

Luistro then called on the Vice President to present her defense before the impeachment court, particularly if she means she is contradicting her own SALN entries that she submitted to the Office of the Ombudsman.

“It would be better for her to address these squarely before the impeachment court, so that all her representations will be considered as testimony in court. I think she needs to address her own admission in the SALN,” Luistro said.
“Iyong SALN, hindi naman prosecution ang gumawa. It was the respondent's own admission under oath and it was her own submission as well. We are just relying on her own admission,” Luistro added.
(The prosecution did not make her SALN.) — Reuters

articles.title: Supreme Court declares 2024, 2025 budgets unconstitutional
articles.summary: The SC rules that in so far as the 2024 and 2025 budgets are concerned, the doctrine of operative fact applies. This recognizes the validity of an assailed act prior to the determination of its…

blocks.text: The SC rules that in so far as the 2024 and 2025 budgets are concerned, the doctrine of operative fact applies. This recognizes the validity of an assailed act prior to the determination of its unconstitutionality.

items: The Supreme Court of the Philippines declared the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts unconstitutional due to unauthorized increases in appropriations by Congress.
While the court acknowledged the validity of certain funds under the doctrine of operative fact, it emphasized that this does not protect those responsible from potential legal liabilities.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC), on Tuesday, October 20, declared the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts (GAA), or budget laws, unconstitutional.

“The Supreme Court (SC) declared as unconstitutional, first, the 2024 General Appropriations Act (GAA) because of Congress’ increase of the unprogrammed appropriations by P449.5 billion, which resulted in an increase in the President’s total recommended appropriations; second, Special Provisions 1(a) and (b), Chapter XLIII of the 2026 GAA; and third, the 2025 GAA because of Congress’ increase of the Special Road Fund by P17.99 billion, which also resulted in an increase in the President’s total recommended appropriation,” said the ruling penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen.

The SC en banc granted the petition of former lawmaker Edcel Lagman and partly granted the legal action of former senator Koko Pimentel challenging the increase in unprogrammed appropriations made by Congress in the 2024 budget.
“It declared unconstitutional Republic Act No. (RA) 11975 or the 2024 GAA because the total appropriations were effectively increased by P449.5 billion,” said the SC.

Unprogrammed funds are standby appropriations that may only be used once specific conditions are met, such as when government revenues exceed targets or when foreign grants and loans are on the table.

In its ruling, the High Court also granted the petition filed by Filipinos for Peace, Justice and Progress Movement, Inc. et al., and declared RA No. 12116, or the 2025 budget law, unconstitutional because of the P17.99-billion increase to the Department of Public Works and Highways’ Special Road Fund. The SC said this “resultantly increased” the budget’s total recommended appropriations.

“As regards the P12.75-billion increase to certain agencies’ Special Accounts in the General Fund, these were found to have violated Book VI, Chapter 4, Section 25 of the Administrative Code, which prohibits increasing amounts in special provisions beyond those proposed by the President,” said the SC.

As to the petition questioning the constitutionality or legality of unprogrammed funds itself, the SC only partially granted the challenge filed by Caloocan City 2nd District Representative Edgar Erice and Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima.
The High Court explained that unprogrammed appropriations are not unconstitutional per se, but they need clear limits and safeguards to ensure fiscal discipline, transparency, and accountability.

“They (unprogrammed appropriations) become constitutionally infirm when they lack sufficient standards, effectively granting the executive unchecked spending authority that weakens fiscal discipline and undermines funding for programmed projects when estimated government revenues are not realized,” said the ruling.

But will the funds be returned? The SC ruled that in so far as the 2024 and 2025 budgets are concerned, the doctrine of operative fact applies to these funds. This legal principle recognizes the validity of an assailed act prior to the determination of its unconstitutionality.

“However, the doctrine covers only irreversible programs whose beneficiaries acted in good faith. It does not shield authors, proponents, or implementors from criminal, civil, or administrative liability unless the proper tribunals explicitly find that they acted in good faith,” the SC explained. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Winnipeg teacher stripped of certificate after sending hundreds of messages to student in 'serious breach'
articles.summary: A Winnipeg teacher has been stripped of his licence over a years-long "inappropriately close relationship" with a student that began in a middle school and continued after the student went on to high…

image.caption: A former River East Transcona School Division teacher has forfeited his certificate after an investigation found he exchanged hundreds of texts and messages with a student. After the student completed middle school, the teacher pursued a job at her high school, according to a new report. (CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A Winnipeg teacher has been stripped of his licence over a years-long "inappropriately close relationship" with a student that began in a middle school and continued after the student went on to high school.
Commissioner pulls licences of River East Transcona, Portage la Prairie teachers for inappropriate messages

Robert Gregoire texted the student hundreds of times from his personal phone and over 1,000 times over Microsoft Teams between 2022 and 2024, referring to her variously as "ma belle," "my beautiful," "muffin" and "princess," according to an Oct. 6 disciplinary decision from Manitoba's independent teacher commissioner.
Gregoire fostered "an increasingly personal relationship" and prioritized "his own emotional needs" over the student's well-being, states the report.
"This conduct represents a serious abuse of the trust."
Gregoire's is one of two new disciplinary decisions posted publicly on the commissioner's disciplinary decision dashboard, which was launched earlier this year.

In 2022, Gregoire began an "inappropriately close relationship that crossed professional boundaries" with a Grade 8 student at the middle school where he worked in the River East Transcona School Division.
Gregoire eventually left his post as a teacher at the middle school to follow the student to her new high school in the division in 2024, the decision states.

items: Registry showing disciplinary records of Manitoba teachers now posted online

blocks.text: Between 2022 and 2024, he and the student exchanged over 1,000 Microsoft Teams messages, including during school breaks and vacations, "late at night and in the early hours of the morning," the report states.
Gregoire referred to her as his "favourite student" who was "très spéciale," or very special, according to the discipline report.
He told her he missed her and that getting a message from her after a bad day gave him a smile, and repeatedly requested she visit him at the middle school after she left.

Gregoire invited the student to meet him outside school at restaurants near her high school. He also invited her for ice cream after school, and to meet with him on weekends and on winter break for skating, the report said.
Cautioned by principal

The principal of the middle school where Gregoire worked cautioned him in June 2024 against messaging students and reminded him to only communicate with those he was instructing for educational purposes.

The principal pointed to the division's code of conduct for child protection, which prohibits writing personal text messages to students and offering special treatment, as well as spending time with students outside of school hours, the disciplinary decision says.
Gregoire ignored the principal and kept texting the student, it says.
He notified the student he would pursue a job opportunity at her school. Later, he messaged her that he was happy to learn he would be teaching one of her classes.
In December 2024, Gregoire hugged the student goodbye at the high school, according to the report. The division put him on administrative leave that month.

items: Manitoba commissioner received 94 complaints about teacher misconduct in first 15 months

blocks.text: River East Transcona School Division filed a complaint with Manitoba's independent education commissioner on April 20 of this year. The commissioner's office ordered an investigation the following day and Gregoire was fired.
He subsequently agreed to the facts surfaced through the commissioner's investigation and agreed they constituted professional misconduct.
Gregoire surrendered his teaching certificate in May. It was permanently cancelled after the investigation wrapped.

"The thousands of messages exchanged over several years, together with Mr. Gregoire’s failure to disclose the relationship, demonstrate a sustained and deliberate pattern of misconduct rather than isolated lapses in judgment," the report concludes.
Gregoire took responsibility for his behaviour and expressed remorse, the report adds.
2nd teacher loses licence

Brady Nurse also lost his teacher certification in a recent decision by Manitoba's teacher commissioner for inappropriately communicating with a student, in what was described as "a fundamental breach of a teacher’s duty of care to students."
Nurse was employed in the Portage la Prairie School Division when, between October and December last year, he exchanged texts with a student.
The commissioner's report characterized the messages as "inappropriate communications" involving "a student experiencing circumstances of heightened vulnerability," which Nurse was aware of.
The division launched its own investigation after being approached by RCMP about Nurse on Dec. 9.
Nurse provided copies of texts between him and the student the next day.
A week later, the division asked if there were any other messages that hadn't been disclosed.
Nurse claimed he had provided all of the messages, but when asked specifically about text messages exchanged on Nov. 18, he retrieved more messages that had been deleted.
He was put on leave two days later.
In an interview with division staff in January, Nurse admitted he didn't share every text initially out of concern that some "might be perceived as inappropriate," the report states.
Nurse admitted to his conduct. He resigned in March and surrendered his teaching certificate in May. It has since officially been cancelled.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bryce Hoye is a multi-platform journalist with a background in wildlife biology. He has worked for CBC Manitoba for over a decade with stints producing at CBC's Quirks & Quarks and Front Burner. He was a 2024-25 Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. He is also Prairie rep for outCBC. He has won a national Radio Television Digital News Association award for a 2017 feature on the history of the fur trade, and a 2023 Prairie region award for an audio documentary about a Chinese-Canadian father passing down his love for hockey to the next generation of Asian Canadians.

articles.title: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
articles.summary: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday

blocks.text: India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.

Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupeesvaluation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.

Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.

At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
after newsletter promotion

Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.

Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

items: Two Serbian opposition figures, Vladan Djokic and Rade Bajic, were targeted with cyberespionage tools, including the Pegasus spyware, ahead of Serbia's parliamentary elections.
Citizen Lab and the Share Foundation reported that Djokic's iPhone was hacked, while Bajic received a warning from Apple about potential spyware targeting his phone.
Both men have faced pressure from authorities due to their opposition to the ruling party, with Bajic linking the spyware attack to his involvement in prosecuting government officials.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Two Serbian opposition figures were recently targeted with powerful cyberespionage tools, according to one of the men and a report issued on Monday, October 19, by the Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab.

The incident was the latest of several in which researchers say surveillance technology was used against students, opposition politicians, and others in Serbia, which will hold a parliamentary election on Sunday.

Citizen Lab said on Monday that a joint investigation with the Share Foundation, a digital rights group, determined that Serbian academic Vladan Djokic’s iPhone had been hacked using the Pegasus spyware tool made by Israeli group NSO.

At the same time, former prosecutor Rade Bajic told Reuters he received a warning from Apple on August 13 that his phone had been targeted using “mercenary spyware,” although he and Citizen Lab both said they had been unable to establish with certainty whether he was hacked or how a hack might have happened.

Serbia’s Interior Ministry did not return messages seeking comment. Officials there have previously dismissed allegations of cyberespionage. NSO, which was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 following years of reports of alleged human rights abuses, did not return emails. NSO, which says it only sells to governments, has previously said it would terminate commercial relationships that result in serious wrongdoing.
Apple confirmed having sent a batch of warnings to users on August 13 but did not directly address questions about Bajic’s or Djokic’s cases.
Both men have crossed Serbia’s ruling party, which has been buffeted by two years of student-led anti-corruption protests.

Djokic, the rector of the University of Belgrade, has been under pressure from authorities following his expressions of solidarity with the students. About 20 minutes before this story was published, a pro-government tabloid published an article describing Djokic as a “vulture” and purporting to carry audio of him talking about his political ambitions.

The source of the audio was not explained. Djokic said in a statement that the hacking of his phone “points to a serious attack on my privacy, security, and the integrity of the office of Rector” and called for those behind it to be punished. The statement did not address the article and he did not immediately return an email seeking comment about it.

Bajic said he was involved in prosecuting senior government officials over allegations that they improperly removed cultural protections on a historic Belgrade army compound that an investment company founded by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, had planned to redevelop. Kushner’s company pulled out of the plan late last year, saying it was doing so out of respect for the people of Serbia and the city of Belgrade.
“In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack,” Bajic said.

Last month, the Share Foundation said that at least 14 people, including students, activists and opposition party members, had been targeted with advanced spyware ahead of local ​elections in March. At least one of the devices was compromised using Pegasus, it said. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: ‘I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,’ says Ateneo coach Louie Alas after the Blue Eagles’ dismal first-round run

‘I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,’ says Ateneo coach Louie Alas after the Blue Eagles’ dismal first-round run

items: Ateneo started the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament strong with a 3-1 record but has since lost three consecutive games, leaving them at 3-4 and seventh in the standings.
Head coach Louie Alas expressed disappointment in the team's performance, attributing their struggles to immaturity and a lack of consistency, particularly in the second half of games.
Despite recent losses, Ateneo remains competitive in the league, with the potential to improve in the second round, starting with a home game against FEU.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Ateneo showed flashes of a contender early in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament. Now, head coach Louie Alas wants his Blue Eagles to grow up before their season slips further away.
Ateneo opened the first round with a promising 3-1 record, putting itself among the league’s top teams.
Given the difficult months the program endured following the deaths of student-athletes Divine Adili and Rene Baterbonia, that start was already a significant achievement.
But the Blue Eagles have since lost three straight games, falling to La Salle, FEU and UST, with two of those defeats coming by double-digit margins.
At 3-4 and seventh in the standings, Ateneo finished the first round well below its coach’s expectations.
“I’m disappointed, super disappointed,” Alas said after the Blue Eagles’ 80-68 loss to UST. “My expectations about our record were higher than this.”
Alas pointed to the team’s immaturity, particularly in the second half, when Ateneo has struggled to keep games competitive late in the round.
“Immaturity. It’s immaturity. That’s it,” Alas said. “That’s one thing I really have to improve. We have to become more mature because we are not kids. We have veterans. We are all adults.”
The numbers back up his frustration as Ateneo surrendered at least 80 points in each of its final three games of the first round, while holding opponents below that mark in all three of its wins.
The Blue Eagles allowed the second-most points per game in the league at 81.14, trailing only the winless UE Red Warriors, who gave up 91.71 per contest.

Kieffer Alas, Louie’s 19-year-old son, has led the Blue Eagles with averages of 14.43 points, 4.57 rebounds, 2.43 assists, and 1.57 steals per game. However, he has shot just 34.55% from the field and 20.57% from three-point range.
Jared Bahay has also had difficulty finding his rhythm, averaging 13.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 4.29 assists while shooting below 40% from the field in the opening round.
His 1-of-13 shooting performance against UST was his worst outing of the first seven games.
Shawn Tuano, Andrew Bongo, Travis Roberts, and Ian Espinosa have likewise struggled to find consistent form, leaving Ateneo searching for more reliable contributions across the roster.
Alas plans to intensify the Blue Eagles’ preparations and practice on top of making the adjustments needed to get them back on track.
“I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,” Alas said. “I know they can do a lot better. Maybe we just have to adjust a bit to our practices.”
“I know they can get it right.”
Despite their three-game skid, Ateneo remains within reach of the teams ahead of it in the standings, as a couple of wins to start the second round could quickly change the Blue Eagles’ position.
The Blue Eagles will have home-court advantage to begin the second round when they host the FEU Tamaraws on Saturday, October 24, at the Blue Eagle Gym. – Rappler.com

articles.title: After lower budget in House version, DepEd asks Senate for P147 billion more
articles.summary: The school-based feeding program and ARAL are among the Department of Education programs that may receive higher funding from the Senate

blocks.text: DEPED BUDGET. Education Secretary Sonny Angara presents the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Education on October 16, 2026.
Department of Education
The school-based feeding program and ARAL are among the Department of Education programs that may receive higher funding from the Senate

items: The Department of Education is requesting an additional P147.93 billion from lawmakers to support its various programs in 2027.
Key funding priorities include nutrition and learning recovery programs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – With the Senate now focusing on passing its own version of the 2027 budget bill, the Department of Education (DepEd) is seeking support for an additional P147.93 billion to implement its programs next year.

This comes as the DepEd only got P967.23 billion in the House of Representatives’ version of the 2027 general appropriations bill (GAB). This is lower than the P976 billion under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

Senator Bam Aquino, who led a budget briefing as chairperson of the Senate finance subcommittee B last Friday, October 16, said his colleagues want an education budget that would reach 4% of the country’s gross domestic product.
Here are some programs that senators may provide higher funding for next year:

Among Aquino’s priorities is putting more money into the DepEd’s school-based feeding program. It has an P11.43-billion allocation in the House’s GAB — the same level in the NEP — but it is significantly lower than the P25.7 billion in the 2026 national budget.
In his presentation, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said the DepEd is seeking P16.82 billion more to at least implement a 180-day feeding cycle for kindergarten and Grade 1.
Senators have a more ambitious move: to provide universal feeding from kindergarten through Grade 3, with a higher unit cost of P30 per meal from the current P25, and a longer cycle of 200 days.
According to DepEd projections, that proposed setup would need an additional P46.65 billion.

blocks.caption: Photo from Department of Education

blocks.text: Aquino had asked for budget scenarios as a bicameral conference committee is set to be convened in the coming weeks for the proposed Expanded National Nutrition Program Act.

“This is one of the biggest reforms that we can do. And if we are able to implement it well, I expect that in three to six years our learning gap problems will be mitigated,” Aquino said in a mix of English and Filipino.
Senators are also expected to inject more funds into the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning or ARAL Program as part of efforts to address the country’s learning crisis.

blocks.caption: PISA 2025 reality: Nearly 2 in 3 Filipino students are ‘low performers’

blocks.text: During the House deliberations, Angara had pointed out that there was zero funding for the ARAL Program in the NEP. In the House’s GAB, lawmakers only provided P255.6 million for the compensation of external tutors and P94.4 million for program management.
Angara said the DepEd needs P15.63 billion for program implementation next year. Asked for a minimum amount, he cited at least P8.9 billion, or the same level in the 2026 budget.
Senators criticized the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) for not funding the ARAL Program in the first place.
Senate President Win Gatchalian said it was “shocking.” Senator Joel Villanueva called it “stupid.”
Senator Erwin Tulfo said the DBM must review the ARAL Law as it states that funds for the program should be included in the annual General Appropriations Act.

DBM Director Vivien Labastilla explained that while there is no line item for the ARAL Program, funding for it is included in the budget for textbooks and other instructional materials and the DepEd’s basic education curriculum.
Angara maintained it was not. “I think the confusion stems from the fact that they are assuming that it’s already subsumed in our regular budget,” he added.
Aquino also said another priority is funding programs related to school safety, especially since the Senate already passed a bill that institutionalizes a comprehensive school safety framework.
Aside from providing equipment like CCTV camera and metal detectors, the Senate is also eyeing child protection training for parents and student leaders.
The DepEd has a total request of P8.18 billion for school safety and security. The House only provided P500 million to hire security guards.

The full breakdown of the DepEd’s budget request to the Senate is found below. Those highlighted in green are items that were given funding in the House’s GAB, while those in yellow are new appeals or items with a higher requested amount compared to the list previously presented to the House.

blocks.caption: Photo from Department of Education
Photo from Department of Education

blocks.text: Updates on classroom construction are also expected to be tackled in the plenary. During the briefing, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) reported that there have been failed biddings on their end.

Under the 2026 national budget, around P65.4 billion was allocated to build 18,960 classrooms this year. Of the amount, P21.45 billion was lodged under the agreement between the DPWH and the DepEd to construct 6,000 classrooms.

DPWH Undersecretary Lara Esquibil told senators that only around P1.87 billion, covering the construction of 533 classrooms, have prospective bidders, while the agency is still advertising P7 billion worth of projects, or around 2,000 classrooms.
“They’ve been concerned with the costing of classrooms with fuel price increases,” Esquibil said.
Aquino suggested transferring the remaining funding of nearly P13 billion to the DepEd so that local government units (LGUs) can instead lead the construction projects.
From the target 10,671 classrooms under the LGU-led construction modality, Angara said over 8,000 classrooms are already in the procurement stage.
Aquino will defend the DepEd’s budget in the plenary on November 24. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Man facing three charges over alleged attack on MP Helen Haines
articles.summary: Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after the incident in Wangaratta

blocks.text: Helen Haines’ alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
He will be held overnight to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday, Victoria police confirmed in a statement, adding that it would be alleged the attack was targeted.

Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after he allegedly struck the independent MP for Indi with a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in northern Victoria.

Haines remains in a critical but stable condition after being airlifted to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery. She has lost one leg and surgeons were fighting on Tuesday to save the other leg.
Police also said in the statement released late on Tuesday that one of its highway patrol officers responded to the incident only eight seconds after emergency services were called.
They confirmed that a search warrant had been executed that morning at Nugent’s Great Alpine Road property.
“Victoria Police will continue to maintain an enhanced presence in Wangaratta, including members from the Public Order Response Team who have deployed to the area.

articles.title: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand
articles.summary: Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming…

image.caption: Traditional German family-owned businesses and SMEs have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investorsImage: Philipp Reinhard/ebm-papst

blocks.text: What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.
Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.
No successor, but an investor instead

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."
"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.
Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.
In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.
Fewer acquisitions, but more investments

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.
Young startups — Germany's next tech champions?

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.
The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.
The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.
Waiting for reforms

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.
Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.
Where are all of Germany's inventors?
At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.
According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.
In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."
This article was originally written in German.
