articles.title: Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy
articles.summary: As Berlin opens a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors, here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

image.caption: A huge, highly revered golden statue of Genghis Khan is found in Mongolia's Chinggis Khaan National Museum, which opened in October 2022 Image: Chinggis Khaan National Museum

blocks.text: Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols."
The power of a disruptive individual
The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader: "If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person."

blocks.caption: Genghis Khan is revered in Mongolia as the founding father of the nation who united the warring steppe tribes. This statue is in the  Parliament Building in Ulan Bator Image: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The founder of the world's largest empire

Genghis Khan was born as Temüjin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temüjin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.
Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

blocks.caption: Nomadic culture, with yurt tents, traditional costumes and music instruments is celebrated here in Mongolia's 'Mongols Nomadic Winter Festival'Image: AFP

blocks.text: Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.
A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.
Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.
A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.
Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

blocks.caption: The 'paiza' acted as the world's earliest form of passport, granting official travelers protection and safe passage across EurasiaImage: Uuganbaatar Otgonbaatar/Chinggis Khaan National Museum, Ulaanbaatar

blocks.text: The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.
Shifting centers of power
The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.
It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies. "When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

blocks.caption: The Mongols also used deception to confuse and trap their opponentsImage: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin – Preußischer Kulturbesitz, Orientabteilung, Diez A fol. 71 S. 58

blocks.text: The Mongols' Western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.
But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we that we still feel the consequences of it today."
The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.
Edited by Helen Whittle

articles.title: Why Israeli Gen Z voters are drawn to the far right
articles.summary: More than half a million young people will cast their ballots in Israel next week - and they could make all the difference.

blocks.text: Far-right minister Ben Gvir (left) has significant support among Israeli youth
ByLucy Williamson
Middle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem
When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme.
His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers.

On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards.
At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote.
"We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country"

blocks.text: Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country"
More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.
Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.

More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.
And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network.
"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle.
"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing."
"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav.
"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."

Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice.
"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next week

blocks.text: Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next week

Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis.

Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.
As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks.
"I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people."
The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks.
But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that.
"For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me.

"They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matter

blocks.text: Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matter
A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis.

The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website.

Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions.
In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference.
Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc

"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett.
He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians.
"The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena."
Shalev said he had pushed his own party to reach young voters through social media.

"Three months ago, Ben Gvir was still the politician with the most amount of views on TikToks, the most amount of likes on TikTok, and Instagram as well," he explained. "Right now, Naftali Bennett is leading [that]."

His boss's Instagram page now features videos of the former prime minister lifting weights to rap music, or chatting with Shalev in the street. Even Netanyahu has joined in with a fast-paced militaristic social media video set to heavy beats.
"Younger people don't watch the news in Israel, [they] don't read the newspapers. The younger generation is getting all its details from TikTok and Instagram".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Beyachad candidate Yonatan Shalev says Ben Gvir understood social media's power sooner than others

blocks.text: Beyachad candidate Yonatan Shalev says Ben Gvir understood social media's power sooner than others
Yahlee Reske and Mika Magal, both 21 years old, rushed out of a nearby bar when they saw Shalev walk past.
"I love him," Mika told me.
"Yes," agreed Yahlee. "He's our age, he's so young and knows so much. It's hard to listen to people who are old and saying the same things over and over again."
Yahlee said she was doing national military service when the 7 October attacks unfolded.
"I don't think I ever looked at politics until then," she said. "But maybe if the government had been different on 7 October, things would have been better."

The same poll suggesting 16% of first-time voters would back a far-right party also suggested that Beyachad alone would take almost 9% of their votes, as would the centre-right Yashar party of Gadi Eisenkot.
At a student event in Tel Aviv last weekend, Ben Gvir was interrupted by protesters shouting, "Fascism will not pass", and forced off the stage.

Israel's young voters may be moving to the right, but they are still as divided as their country, over who they believe is the guardian of Israel's security and identity, and who is an existential threat.
Additional reporting by Morgan Gisholt Minard and Gidi Kleiman

articles.title: France plans 'massive' weekend police surge amid protests
articles.summary: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told parliament the government would respond and reinforce police in major cities. He also accused extreme-left groups of trying to hijack what began as…
articles.byline: Mahima Kapoor, Roshni Majumdar, Matt Ford

image.caption: Several cities, including Paris, the southwestern city of Bordeaux and Nice on the French Riviera, introduced partial curfews on MondayImage: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 20, 2026
France's Lecornu accuses 'far-left' of 'insurrectionary plan' to escalate protests

blocks.caption: PM Lecornu told parliament that the police presence would be larger, more mobile and better supported next weekendImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

blocks.text: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has told French lawmakers that authorities would mobilize a "massive" security presence next weekend, after organizers announced plans for new protests.
"The deployment for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu said in the National Assembly.
He said the security operation last weekend had been "too static and not mobile enough."

Lecornu said adequate support for security forces was "the precondition for everything" when trying to both allow peaceful protests but also keep order, saying that "1,000 injured police and gendarmes over the weekend" nationwide was unacceptable.
Lecornu said the national public message in response should convey to them "clear, frank and massive support."

The prime minister also accused what he referred to as small ultra-left and extreme-left groups in certain locations of forging an "insurrectionary plan" that fueled the violent rioting over the weekend for which the government could provide evidence.

"What happened at the mayoral office of Limoges was an example. You have a first arrest that was carried out this morning," Lecornu said. "This individual arrested is, unfortunately, already known to [security] services."

He said authorities would not tolerate such groups "marching on the Elysee or Matignon," referring to the offices and residences of President Emmanuel Macron and himself as head of government, and saying that some of these groups had harbored such ambitions.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Video of people panic-buying water drums for Super El Niño is AI-generated
articles.summary: Multiple satirical videos surfaced online after Marcos advised people to buy buckets to store water amid concerns over Super El Niño

blocks.text: Claim: Hordes of people are panic-buying water drums at a local warehouse after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. advised the public to store water in preparation for the anticipated Super El Niño.
Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user Bonz Gimenez posted a viral video showing hundreds of people supposedly storming a water drum warehouse to hoard multiple containers.
The caption read, “Panic buying ng mga malalaking drums sa isang warehouse (Panic buying of large drums at a warehouse).”

The individuals in the video appeared hysterical, arguing over the plastic drums and pushing each other. Vehicles are scattered around the supposed warehouse, where people are shown loading the containers.
The video has garnered 20 million views, 257,000 reactions, 10,400 comments, and 26,000 shares as of writing.

While multiple commenters believe the video to be AI-generated, many still believe the claim. One Facebook user commented, “Hala? Ante Claire [Castro] at BBM (Marcos), nag-panic buying na ng mga drum at timba; ang galing niyo talaga!”
(Oh my? Auntie Claire and BBM, people have started panic-buying drums and pails — you guys are truly something else!)
Multiple users have also reposted the video, claiming it was the result of the President’s advice to the public to buy buckets to collect rainwater in preparation for the effects of Super El Niño.

The facts: The video is AI-generated. SightEngine, an AI detection tool, flagged screenshots of the video as 99% likely to be AI-generated. It also gave the video a score of 32%, with some frames reaching 66% and 99%. Similarly, Hive Detect also marked multiple parts of the video as 81% AI-generated.
There are also no reports from credible sources confirming the incident shown in the video.
The video and other satirical content about plastic water buckets were fueled by the President’s statement during an interview in Singapore on October 11.

While talking about the government’s plans to prepare for the anticipated water supply issue with the looming Super El Niño, Marcos said, “Bumili na kayo ng balde para ‘pag umulan, makolekta na ninyo lahat.”
(Buy buckets so when it rains, you can collect rainwater).
He added that the government would roll out an information campaign on filtering and storing rainwater, saying, “We’ll give you the filter; we’ll teach you how to do everything.”

Marcos’ bucket remark has drawn mixed reactions, but Palace Press Officer Claire Castro clapped back at government detractors in an October 13 statement, saying: “Hindi po ito pagkaniya-kaniya. Kung ito lang po ang narinig na patungkol sa balde, ang mas maganda po, umupo sila at makinig. Sit down and listen kung ano ang sinasabi ng Pangulo.”

(This is not about everyone fending for themselves. If all they heard was the remark about buckets, it would be better if they sat down and listened. Sit down and listen to what the President is saying.)
She added that Marcos’ advice was not a joke and should be taken seriously.
Meanwhile, Vice President Sara Duterte said on October 12 that she does not want to comment about Marcos’ bucket statement, but mentioned that “we can’t rely on the President.”

Water filtration: In an October 14 Palace briefing, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said it would distribute water filtration kits to communities vulnerable to El Niño, then demonstrated how to use them.

The DSWD will first distribute the kits to local government units that have declared a state of calamity due to El Niño, as well as high-density areas in Metro Manila experiencing low water pressure. (READ: DENR: 1 in 3 barangays nationwide highly vulnerable to El Niño)
Since 2024, the department has already deployed buckets with built-in water filtration technology to disaster-hit areas without access to potable water.
Higher demand: Markets are already seeing a high demand for buckets and water drums. Stores in Divisoria have begun procuring more supplies as people buy more than usual.

Vendors have assured the public that supplies remain available, even as one seller urged consumers to avoid panic buying. The government has also echoed this, as police continue to monitor the situation.

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration, the current El Niño is expected to intensify into a very strong El Niño between the September–December 2026 season and persist through the first half of 2027. – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

articles.title: A contractor left this Toronto man without a roof. His insurance company is denying his claim
articles.summary: What began as a simple knock on the front door last spring has resulted in an elderly Scarborough man living out of a suitcase, his home roofless and in ruins. While police are investigating a…

image.caption: Lawrence Huang says he has been living in motels since contractors walked off the job after removing his roof. He says he has no way to pay for the rebuild, as his insurance company has denied his claim. (Michael Smee/CBC)

blocks.text: What began as a simple knock on the front door last spring has resulted in an elderly Scarborough man living out of a suitcase, his home roofless and in ruins.
Police are now investigating a possible fraud, while the man's home insurance company has denied most of his claim.

Lawrence Huang was approached in late May by representatives of a company called Super Dry Roofing and Masonry, who told him his roof was infested with rodents, seriously damaged, and in need of replacement.
The 76-year-old, whom his niece Katie Semple describes as “on the spectrum,” signed a roof replacement contract and gave a salesman for the company a $25,000 advance on the $50,000 job.
The contractor went to work, completely removing the roof of Huang’s two-storey Guildwood Parkway home, leaving the contents open to the elements.

The kitchen of Lawrence Huang's home, four months after contractors left the job site, with the home's roof removed. TD Insurance has said it will cover the cost of the home's ruined contents, but not the structural damage. (Mike Smee/CBC)

And the price began to rise. Semple says her uncle then handed over $1,800. Within weeks he gave the contractor another cheque, this time for $64,000 — at which point employees at his bank became suspicious, and refused to honour the large cheque. They also contacted police, the city and Semple, his only surviving relative.
Within days, the workers abruptly abandoned the site, leaving his home with no roof and a massive pile of scrap lumber in the driveway.
Semple says she has tried to contact Super Dry, but the phone number appears to be disconnected.
CBC Toronto has also attempted to contact the company using phone and email contacts listed on the contract. The phone number is not assigned and an email was returned as undeliverable.
Insurance won't cover 'faulty ... workmanship'

After Super Dry left, Huang initially tried living in the basement, but city engineers and Toronto Fire Service ordered him to leave. Since then, Semple says, he has been living in motels and trying to figure out how his home can be rebuilt — and how it will all be paid for.
The contents of his home, including valuable books and family mementoes, are now a sodden mess, destroyed by trespassers, rain and animals.
“It’s a lifetime of memories,” Semple said. “It’s terrible. I lost sleep. I don’t know what to do. I’m the only one he has left.”
Katie Semple stands in what was once the living room of her uncle's Scarborough home. She says trespassers have done damage, as has the weather. (Mike Smee/CBC)
Semple says her uncle’s insurer, TD Insurance, is refusing to cover most of the damage, including Huang’s rebuild, which he cannot afford to do on his own.

In a Sept. 9 letter to Huang, shared with CBC Toronto, TD Insurance’s adjuster wrote: “We do not insure the cost of correcting faulty design, material or workmanship.” Damage caused by animals, vandalism or rain also isn't covered in Lawrence Huang's policy, according to the letter.
Semple argues that, in her opinion, the damage to the home was caused by a fraudulent company — but, she says, TD Insurance still isn’t budging on paying for the damage to the roof.

TD Insurance wouldn't speak with CBC Toronto about Huang’s case, citing privacy concerns. But in an email, the company wrote: “TD Insurance recognizes how distressing this situation has been for our client and his family and continues to work directly with them regarding the claim."

Lawrence Huang says he initially tried to live in the basement of his home after the contractor left mid-project, but Toronto Fire Service and city engineers said he had to move out. (Michael Smee/CBC)

Semple says she hired her own adjuster to communicate with the company and some progress has been made. In a follow-up letter dated Sept. 28, TD Insurance said it will cover the damage to the contents after all, but remains adamant that it will not pay for the home’s rebuild.
Until that happens, Huang will continue to live in a motel. Semple says he is covering those costs, but he doesn’t have enough money to rebuild the house.

Luis Seco, a University of Toronto professor who studies the insurance industry, says it’s common for insurers to balk at covering some types of damage, typically structural, which is the most expensive to repair.

items: Home damaged in the GTA storm? Here are your options
A fire destroyed their home. Now they can’t get emergency housing because they have a dog

blocks.text: He says ultimately an insurance company can deny any claim, and the onus is then on the homeowner to take them to court, if they believe the company is violating its policy contract.

But that can be expensive, and he suggests that homeowners first apply to a non-profit insurance industry mediator, the General Insurance Ombudservice, whose members include most Canadian insurance companies.
Police investigating, say roofing scams common
Toronto police acknowledged in an email that it is investigating a fraud complaint at Huang’s property.
Det. David Coffey of the financial crimes unit told CBC Toronto he couldn't comment on Huang’s case specifically, but he said roofing scams are common in the city.
“We’ve been dealing with roofing scams for as long as I've been a police officer, and that’s 29 years,” he said.
Det. David Coffey is with Toronto Police Services' financial crimes unit. He says confidence schemes have cost Torontonians $50 million so far this year. (Mike Smee/CBC)
He said the roofing scam is considered a con game, in which a fraudster builds up a person’s confidence before talking them out of their money.

Typically the scam begins with a salesperson’s knock on the door. The homeowner is warned that a leak in his or her roof is imminent and urgently needs fixing. “They present themselves as the answer to that emergency,” Coffey said. “Your roof is going to leak and the city is going to condemn your house.”
He said most scammers begin by asking for relatively small sums — in the low thousands — and then they escalate the demand until they're convinced the homeowner has nothing left to give.
“It’s really the urgency and the fear they’re generating,” Coffee says. “We’re not reacting intellectually; we’re reacting emotionally.”

So far this year, Coffey says cons of all types have cost Torontonians about $50 million. And that only covers reported scams. TPS figures only about five to 10 percent of victims actually report the crime.
'Bring yourself down off that ledge'
Coffey says the damage done to the Huang home — if it is a fraud — would be “on the higher end” of the typical roofing scam.
His advice? “You need to bring yourself down off that ledge they’ve put you on … Pause and verify. Slow it down and do your own due diligence into that company.”
But he says the best defence is to simply not do business with contractors who come knocking.
“Personally, as a citizen, I wouldn't hire anyone who knocks on my door," Coffey said.
“Urgency these days doesn't mean hurry up. Urgency these days has to mean stop, and verify and talk to your family, talk to other people. Those are the keys.”

articles.title: Incoming Quebec premier asks lieutenant-governor to skip cabinet's swearing-in
articles.summary: In a letter sent Monday to Lt.-Gov. Manon Jeannotte, the Parti Québécois leader stated his incoming government will not allow a representative of the British Crown to preside over the event.

image.caption: PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already stated he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to King Charles. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
In a letter sent Monday to Lt.-Gov. Manon Jeannotte, the Parti Québécois leader stated his incoming government will not allow a representative of the British Crown to preside over the event.
Court to hear emergency bid to force newly elected Quebec politicians to swear oath to monarch
Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has formally asked the province's lieutenant-governor to stay away from his new cabinet’s swearing-in ceremony on Wednesday.
"We firmly intend to abolish this monarchy in Quebec, both within our democratic institutions and in our civil society," St-Pierre Plamondon wrote.

He makes it clear that he does not want the lieutenant-governor present, requesting that she sign the necessary appointment documents behind the scenes so the Secretary General can administer the oaths without her. Proceeding this way, the PQ leader wrote, will allow the newly appointed ministers to begin their work immediately.

“We thank you in advance for the co-operation you will demonstrate to ensure that this important day for our democracy unfolds without hindrance and with respect for the will of the elected members of the National Assembly of Quebec,” he added.
But the new government's anti-monarchy agenda is facing an immediate legal roadblock.
One of the lawyers challenging the 2022 Quebec law that made the mandatory oath to the King optional for elected officials says his case for an emergency injunction will be heard in court Tuesday.
Lawrence David said in an email he expects a quick decision from Judge Ian Demers, but "we will 100 per cent appeal the judgment if we do not win."
To swear or not to swear allegiance

Earlier this month, David, founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, filed an emergency injunction in an attempt to force the incoming Parti Québécois (PQ) government to swear allegiance to King Charles.

The injunction asks the court to immediately suspend a 2022 provincial law, known as Bill 4, that made the oath to the monarch optional for members of the National Assembly. David already filed a lawsuit in August over the same matter.

items: Injunction filed to force incoming PQ government to take oath to King

blocks.text: Bill 4 added a clause to the Constitution Act of 1867 stating that the oath to the monarch no longer applies to Quebec legislators.

The bill was tabled by the Coalition Avenir Québec government after facing pressure from the PQ. Several members of the PQ had refused to swear allegiance to King Charles III and were barred from sitting.
Will the PQ be barred from their seats?

The legal challenge comes on the heels of the provincial election, which handed the Parti Québécois a minority government. St-Pierre Plamondon has already stated he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to King Charles.
If the stay is granted, incoming MNAs who refuse the oath could be legally barred from taking their seats when the legislature reconvenes in mid-November.

At the heart of the lawsuit is the argument that Quebec unilaterally altered the 1867 Constitution Act without the required unanimous consent of the House of Commons, the Senate and all of the country’s provincial legislatures to abolish the mandatory oath.

items: PQ leader readies team for the work ahead as members sworn in at National Assembly

blocks.text: It also alleges the law violates Section 3 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees the right to effective representation, because politicians who do not take the oath are not qualified to serve as an MNA.
David has warned that if the newly elected government attempts to unilaterally abolish the office of the lieutenant-governor, he is prepared to launch additional legal challenges.
Written by Isaac Olson

articles.title: Japan probe sets course for Mars moon
articles.summary: The MMX spacecraft is on its way to Mars' moon Phobos to collect surface samples that could help answer long-standing questions about the formation of the Solar System.

image.caption: Thousands of people tuned into the livestream of the launch despite the early hour in JapanImage: Kyodo/REUTERS

blocks.text: A Japanese spacecraft successfully set off on a journey to one of Mars' moons late Monday in a race to become the first mission to return samples to Earth and potentially unlock the mysterious origins of the Solar System.

The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is expected to reach Mars in August 2027. It will attempt to collect samples from Phobos, the larger of the planet's two moons, and deploy the German-French rover IDEFIX to explore the surface.
Pioneering mission heads to Mars moon — and back

The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX probe lifted off into a pitch-black sky from the Tanegashima Space Center at 4:41 a.m. local time (1941 GMT Monday), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) said.

Flight controllers burst into applause and jumped to their feet as the spacecraft blasted into space, shaking hands and embracing. Thousands of people tuned in to watch the livestream despite the early hour.
An hour later, JAXA announced that the probe had successfully separated from the H3 rocket and was "beginning its journey towards the Martian system."
"I'd dreamt of this day, so I'm incredibly happy," said JAXA scientist Mari Aida. "Right now I feel really relieved."
The agency also received signals from the spacecraft as expected, confirming it was operating normally.
Making way for science
Scientists hope the probe's discoveries will help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.

"The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars," Nicky Fox, administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a message broadcast on the JAXA live stream.

blocks.caption: The mission is a collaboration with US and European space agencies, as well as numerous universities and tech companiesImage: Kyodo/REUTERS

blocks.text: JAXA also hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, unlocking a key piece of knowledge about the formation of the Solar System.

One theory holds that Mars' two moons formed after a giant celestial body collided with the planet. Another hypothesis suggests the moons are asteroids captured by Mars' gravity. Confirming either theory would help scientists determine "how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets," JAXA said, referring to the four rocky planets closest to the sun.
Probe to reach destination in August 2027
The probe is due to arrive near Mars around August 2027, where it will orbit one of the planet's two natural moons, Phobos.

A French-German rover named IDEFIX, after the dog from the Asterix comic series, will be the first vehicle to travel across Phobos to conduct surface observations and help ensure a safe landing for the Japanese probe. It is no bigger than a microwave oven.

Once MMX arrives on Phobos, it will spend about two hours collecting at least 10 grams of material from the moon's surface before launching back into space. It will also study Mars' other natural moon, Deimos, during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian region in 2030.

blocks.caption: Phobos, the larger of the two Martian moons, orbits the planet three times a dayImage: JAXA/DLR/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another objective of the mission is to explore the possibility of using Phobos as a "natural space station" by establishing the requirements for a round trip.
Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock measuring about 22 kilometers (14 miles) across.
The mission, which aims to complete the first round trip to the Martian region, is a collaboration involving US and European space agencies along with several private technology companies.

US and Chinese space agencies have also been competing to become the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars to Earth. NASA's Perseverance rover, which has been exploring the planet since 2021, has already collected samples. The return mission, however, was canceled by US President Donald Trump's administration after a congressional vote in January.

articles.title: She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home
articles.summary:
​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism

Before 24 July, a person I will…

blocks.text: Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.

That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.

“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.

The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.

I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.

The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them.

R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.

After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.

Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)
“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”

But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.

“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”

With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.
During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.

Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.
“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.
R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.

Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue.)

R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.
“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.
Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.

It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A still from award-winning film Selvi.

blocks.text: Culture | Two Indian films won awards at the Busan international film festival. Birds in the Dark by Shashank Walia was awarded the Songwon Vision audience prize and Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi won the HyLife Vision as well as the Taipei Film Commission award.

Politics | The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, will land in Mumbai on 20 October for his second visit to India this year. Rubio will meet foreign minister S Jaishankar and then travel to Jamnagar, home to Reliance Industries’ massive refinery.

Imran Khan | Days after the Bollywood actor Imran Khan appeared at a Mumbai protest against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, authorities asked him to leave the country by 28 October over what they described as a violation of the Foreigners Act. The action followed a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya against Khan, who is a US citizen.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Media Ka Loktantra by Vineet Kumar. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: With the chief justice of India criticising citizen journalist covering the recent protests, veteran television reporter Ravish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.

“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s book Media Ka Loktantra (Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: The National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) plant in Dadri. Photograph: Prakash Singh/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Close to 45% of thermal power plants in India – as many as 84 out of 191 – were critically low on coal stocks (£) as of early October. At the same time, the country’s demand for power grew by 10% this year, the highest year-on-year increase in the past 10 years.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: A felt sculpture by Sagarika Sundaram at the Henry Moore Institute. Photograph: Rob Harris

blocks.text: Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.

“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.

The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.

articles.title: Brendan Nugent’s family say Helen Haines has been their friend for more than 20 years
articles.summary:
Father of 43-year-old Tarrawingee man who allegedly attacked the independent MP say incident is ‘devastating and unfathomable’

  • Follow our

blocks.text: The father of a 43-year-old man accused of allegedly attacking Helen Haines has pledged to work with police and described the incident as “shocking and horrific”.

The independent MP remained in a critical condition on Tuesday after being airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night. She has lost one leg, with surgeons working to save the other.
Police confirmed a 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene.
In a statement, Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and Rod’s partner, Christine Cunningham, said Haines had been their friend for more than 20 years.
“What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” they said.

“We would like to sincerely thank members of the local community and police who came to Helen’s aid yesterday after the shocking and horrific crime. We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.
“Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community.”
Guardian Australia has spoken to local residents who have been concerned about Nugent’s behaviour for several years, including multiple allegations of abuse and threats from him.
They reported erratic behaviour, shouting and music playing loudly until the early hours of the morning. They also raised concerns about his mental health.
Nugent is a long-term forestry campaigner in the state’s north-east. Environment campaigners who worked with Nugent several years ago have expressed shock at his arrest.

Nugent has a master’s of forest ecosystems science from the University of Melbourne and spent years researching the forestry industry in Victoria. He has also been a registered business owner in Wangaratta.
Nugent was a committee member for the Save our Strathbogie Forest group, which campaigns against logging in the region. He became inactive around 2019-20.
His arrest has shocked the group’s chair, Bertrant Lobert, who said he initially appeared to be “a reasonable and thoughtful person but then he drifted away”.
“He was engaging, he was thoughtful and to hear what has happened now, if it all turns out to be true, is just completely shocking,” Lobert said.
“This is quite personal as a lot of people in our group knew Helen personally and were friends.
“This is more than just a tragedy about the targeting of public figures, it’s about our community and the people we know.”
Helen McKernan, the president of the Strathbogie Ranges Conservation Management Network Inc, also worked with Nugent as an activist before 2020.
She says Nugent lost contact with her network of forestry campaigners around this date.
“He was a committed activist,” McKernan said. “He would sleep out if necessary and help behind the scenes. We could always rely on him to turn up and contribute.”
after newsletter promotion
“It’s just a shock.”

When the then-Victorian minister for environment, Lily D’Ambrosio, visited the Strathbogie forest in November 2019 to announce a ban on native forest logging, Nugent was among a group of about a dozen environmentalists who posed for photos.
Also among the group was Rebecca Swift, a friend of Dezi Freeman who owned the property where he was living when two police officers were killed and a third injured in a shooting last year.
Swift and Freeman shared conspiratorial beliefs about government and the Covid-19 pandemic, but it is unclear whether Nugent also embraced those views.
“Lily I was so pleased to be in the Strathbogie forest to hear your announcement today,” Swift commented on D’Ambrosio’s Facebook post announcing the logging ban.

“You gave us heart and hope that we are heard, and that our beloved wild landscapes are valued for so much more than merely dollars. Forest and wildlife defenders welcome a future where we can assist genuine governments to care for our national parks.”
Swift was contacted for comment.
The Victorian Nationals MP Tim McCurdy said Nugent was known to his Wangaratta office and regularly came in to raise different issues.
“He’s been at our office,” McCurdy said. “We get plenty of people come in, half a dozen a day come for various things. So yes, he’s been into our office, [to raise] various issues.
“Our office didn’t feel threatened by him, if they had they would ring the police. I want to wish Helen all the best.”
In October 2019, when Nugent was still actively campaigning on forestry issues, he praised Haines for her stance on climate change.
When Haines posted on X about an ABC Q+A episode, Nugent wrote “Would’ve been nice to include a politician who takes climate change seriously, such as yourself”.
– with AAP

3 killed in attack on Meitei villagers in India's Manipur state
At least three people were killed when suspected militants alleged to be from the ethnic Kuki community opened fire on 14 villagers from the Meitei community in India's northeastern state of Manipur.
The Meitei villagers were cutting and transporting firewood when the alleged attack took place, Lhari Dorjee Lhatoo, a senior police official, told reporters.
"Three individuals succumbed to bullet injuries. Others sustained injuries and are undergoing further medical treatment," Lhatoo told Reuters.
Meitei groups have blamed "militants" from the Kuki community for the attack, while Kuki groups have denied the allegations.
India's Manipur conflict fuels demands for separate state
The incident sparked protests in the state capital, Imphal, with villagers carrying two bodies to the residence of the chief minister.

Bordering Myanmar, Manipur is home to various ethnic communities. The hilly state has witnessed ethnic violence between its mostly Hindu Meitei majority and largely Christian Kuki minority since 2023 over economic benefits and job quotas.

articles.title: Canada: Alberta rejects separation bid, CBC projects
articles.summary: Voters have decisively rejected a proposal to begin the legal process toward Alberta's independence, dealing a major blow to a movement driven largely by economic grievances.

image.caption: Voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta delivered a strong endorsement of remaining in CanadaImage: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canada's Alberta province has overwhelmingly rejected a plan to begin the process of seeking independence from Canada.

Canadian public broadcaster CBC projects a decisive victory for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76% support for remaining in Canada after roughly a third of the votes had been counted.
The nonbinding referendum asked residents whether they wanted to stay in Canada or start the legal steps needed for a future binding vote on separation.
The vote marks the first separation referendum held outside Quebec, where past independence movements have been driven by language and cultural differences.

In Alberta, the campaign was largely fueled by economic grievances. The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated, with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.

The result is a significant setback for separatist groups and their supporters but a much-needed win for Prime ​Minister Mark Carney as ​he ‌attempts to keep the country unified amid an ongoing trade war with ‌the US.
This is a developing story. Please refresh for updates.

articles.title: Alberta voters reject plan for referendum to leave Canada, CBC projects
articles.summary:
Projection delivers a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward…

blocks.text: Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the national broadcaster CBC has projected, delivering a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity.

With more than 1 million votes counted early Tuesday, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation. About a third of ballots had been counted.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours – but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening, the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.
Prime minister Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government.
“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.
The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, has said publicly that she will vote to remain in Canada, but that she will not require elected members of her party to do the same.

Her tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months, Smith has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.

The referendum has also become a political liability for Smith’s party, which has seen popular support tumble in recent months, including the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold during a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, told the Guardian the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city” amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.
“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” said Farkas.

“And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together because no result will permanently put this to bed,” he added, “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

articles.title: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
articles.summary:
Critics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolation

Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to

blocks.text: Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.

A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.
Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her.

Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital.

Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail.

Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED. Since then, Suu Kyi’s whereabouts and health have been difficult to determine until an International Committee of the Red Cross visit in August.

Coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has been making efforts to rebuild regional and international diplomatic ties.
Kim Aris, Suu Kyi’s son who lives in London, said in a statement that he welcomed Charles’s gifts but warned their delivery should not be exploited by the regime.

“We must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy,” he said. “My mother’s fundamental human rights continue to be violated.”
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington considers a genocide.

The former commander-in-chief has recently conducted several regional visits to rebuild bilateral ties with neighbours, after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) regional bloc barred him from its summits for not following an Asean-brokered ‌peace plan.
During his most recent trip to Malaysia this month, the leader was given an official welcome and honour guard. Min Aung Hlaing earlier visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.

blocks.caption: Aung San Suu Kyi pictured delivering a speech in 2020.  Photograph: Aung Shine Oo/AP

blocks.text: Phil Robertson, director at the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates (AHRLA) group, said the Suu Kyi book photo op was part of Myanmar’s “quest for global legitimacy”.

“The bottom line is Asean has grown tired of arguing with Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s intransigent military leaders and having nothing to show for it, and they desperately want to move the bloc on to other, more cheery issues,” he said.

“So as the Asean dominoes fall to the Myanmar charm offensive, they just want to make their regional capitulation look good – and that requires Myanmar to play its part by trotting out Suu Kyi at occasional intervals to receive their latest beneficence.”
Min Aung Hlaing has also made efforts to reach out to Donald Trump’s administration, saying in a September interview with Time magazine that “it would be ideal if the US could cooperate with us”.

Weeks later, Reuters reported that the US and Myanmar officials had held talks in Naypyidaw and Tokyo, in part to shut down scam centres that target Americans, but which could be broadened to exploitation of Myanmar’s mineral deposits.

The US state department has said it is re-examining “the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country”. China has become Myanmar’s key global partner.

Myanmar has always denied the accusations of genocide, and Suu Kyi, who held the role of state counsellor at the time of the atrocities, defended the country at the international court of justice, disappointing many in her global support base.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
articles.summary: Ahead of the midterms Trump has boasted about the performance of the US economy. BBC Verify looks at inflation, jobs and economic growth in the country.

blocks.text: ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondent
President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.
Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."

While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.
The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.
So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims.
1. US economy growing
The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.
The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.
And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.
That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.

The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.
It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.
Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.
The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.
Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office.
2. Inflation picked up
Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.
The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%.
That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.
Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.
While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.
3. Household income growth held back
Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump.
The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.
However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:
- Trump's tax cuts
- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans
- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war
ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.
The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.
ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.
4. Job creation slowed down
Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.
Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.
​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external.
5. Borrowing costs rising
The growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.
The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.
That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.
The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4%, external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.

That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates, external and cannot take with them to a new property.
Data graphics by Erwan Rivault.
